draft.title: Personification and symbolism
card: gives human actions or feelings to something that is not human. In "the wind sulked around the house", the wind is shown as moody.
Personification makes a scene or object feel alive. It can also shape how a reader feels about it, such as seeing a storm as hostile.
an object, colour or image that stands for a larger idea. A locked gate might stand for being shut out or kept apart.
A symbol gains meaning each time it returns. Each new appearance can add to what it suggests, so readers watch how it changes.
draft.remember: Personification makes things act human. A symbol stands for a bigger idea and builds meaning as it returns.

a.q: Which line is an example of personification?
opts: The old clock grumbled through the long afternoon
The old clock was loud and rusty
The old clock ticked like a dripping tap
The old clock sat on the kitchen shelf
a.why: A clock cannot grumble, so the line gives it a human mood. The simile compares the ticking to a tap, but it does not give the clock a human quality.
a.clue: Look for a human feeling or action given to an object.

b.q: In a short story, Priya's grandmother keeps a red scarf. It appears when the family argues, when they make peace and when the grandmother dies. What makes the scarf a symbol?
opts: It stands for family bonds and gains meaning each time
It is a bright colour that catches the reader's eye
It is described as if the scarf were alive
It is mentioned more than once in the story
b.why: The scarf is tied to a larger idea, the bond within the family, and each return adds to that meaning. Repetition alone is not enough, because an object can be repeated without standing for anything bigger.
b.clue: Ask what bigger idea the scarf points to, and how each return changes it.

a.best: The old clock grumbled through the long afternoon

b.best: It stands for family bonds and gains meaning each time
